name: Horodok
summary: A fortified salt town west of Lviv, first named in 1213, where Władysław II Jagiełło died on 1 June 1434 at the end of a forty-eight-year reign.
overview: A town in the Ruthenian lands west of Lviv, built on salt and on the road, and the place where Władysław II Jagiełło died in 1434.
knownFor: The death of Władysław II Jagiełło on 1 June 1434
Salt springs and a salt staple that gave it the name Solonyi Horodok
A fortified point of Galicia-Volhynia, first recorded in 1213

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Horodok lies about thirty kilometres west of Lviv, on the low watershed country where the rivers begin to run towards the Baltic on one side and the Black Sea on the other. The name simply means a small fortified place, which is what it was: a strongpoint on the road, first named in the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle in 1213 as a well-defended town.

Its wealth came from salt. The springs here supported salt-making and, more profitably, a staple where salt was stored and traded, so that the town was known as Solonyi Horodok, the salt Horodok. In the thirteenth century it was a centre of the salt stores that supplied a wide region.

contentSections.title: From Galicia-Volhynia to the Polish crown
paragraphs: Horodok belonged to the principality of Galicia-Volhynia, the Rus’ successor state that held the south-western lands after the Mongol invasions had broken Kyiv. It was one of the fortified points that gave that principality its shape, and it saw the fighting that came with the contest between Rus’, Polish and Hungarian claims to the region.

In 1349 the town passed with Galicia to Casimir III of Poland, and thereafter it was a royal town on the eastern edge of the Polish kingdom. It received Magdeburg rights in 1389 — the German-derived charter of urban self-government that Polish and Ruthenian towns adopted, giving the burghers their own court and council.

contentSections.title: A king’s stopping place
paragraphs: Władysław II Jagiełło, grand duke of Lithuania and king of Poland, used Horodok repeatedly across his long reign, from 1387 until his death, and he founded a Franciscan house in the town in 1420. This was not sentiment but administration: late medieval kingship was itinerant, and a ruler governing both Poland and Lithuania spent his life moving between them, staying in places like this one because they lay on his road and could feed his household.
That habit is the reason a king of Poland died in an unremarkable Ruthenian town rather than in Kraków, and it is why Horodok appears in the record at all.

contentSections.title: The death of Jagiełło, 1434
paragraphs: In the forty-eighth year of his reign, travelling in the Przemyśl country, the old king caught a chill from which he did not recover. He died at Horodok on 1 June 1434, somewhere past eighty — the precise figure depends on which birth year is accepted, and the sources allow a range of about a decade.

The story attached to the death is that he sat out at night to listen to nightingales and took cold doing it. It is a good story and it belongs to Jan Długosz, the chronicler writing a generation later, so it should be treated as a chronicler’s anecdote rather than a medical record. The bare facts — the journey, the chill, the place and the date — are not in dispute.

His body was carried to Kraków and buried in Wawel Cathedral. His son Władysław III, a boy of ten, was elected king on 25 July 1434, and the dynasty Jagiełło had founded went on to rule Poland and Lithuania for nearly two centuries.

contentSections.title: The town afterwards
paragraphs: Horodok kept the king’s memory in its Polish name, Gródek Jagielloński — Jagiełło’s Gródek — which it bore until the twentieth century. It remained a small trading town, and the salt that made it eventually mattered less as larger sources were worked elsewhere.

Nothing above ground survives from Jagiełło’s visits. The oldest standing churches are later: Saint Nicholas with its bell tower, of 1510, and the Annunciation, of 1633 — buildings that show the town continuing as a Ruthenian religious centre long after the king who died there had been forgotten by everyone but the mapmakers.

timeline.title: First recorded

timeline.title: The salt staple
timeline.description: The town becomes a centre for storing and trading salt, and is known as Solonyi Horodok.

timeline.title: To the Polish crown
timeline.description: Horodok passes with Galicia to Casimir III of Poland.

timeline.title: Magdeburg rights
timeline.description: The town receives the charter of self-government, with its own council and court.

timeline.title: A Franciscan foundation
timeline.description: Władysław II Jagiełło founds a Franciscan house in the town he visited throughout his reign.

timeline.title: Death of Jagiełło
timeline.description: The king dies at Horodok after catching a chill while travelling in the Przemyśl country; he is buried at Wawel Cathedral.

timeline.title: His son elected
timeline.description: The ten-year-old Władysław III is elected king of Poland.

timeline.title: Saint Nicholas church
timeline.description: The oldest surviving church in the town is built, long after the medieval castle and royal lodging have gone.
